analysis.one_liner: Abolishes federal civil asset forfeiture — police taking property without convicting the owner of a crime.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in December 2014 with no cosponsors, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and died there without a hearing or vote when Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ended the federal government's ability to take people's money, homes, cars, and financial assets through civil asset forfeiture — a process where property is seized based on suspected connection to crime, without the owner ever being convicted or even charged. It would have banned federal agencies from joining 'equitable sharing' programs with state and local police and from accepting property seized locally, while still allowing seizure of contraband and forfeiture after a criminal conviction. The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose property could be targeted by federal civil forfeiture: people pulled over with cash, small-business owners whose bank deposits are flagged, and families whose homes or vehicles are seized without the owner being charged or convicted of anything. The bill would shift the burden back to the government and require a criminal conviction before taking property.

how_it_helps.text: It bars seizure or forfeiture of private property under any federal civil asset forfeiture law, allowing forfeiture only for contraband or after a criminal conviction.
It prohibits federal agencies from joining 'equitable sharing' programs or adopting property seized by state and local police, closing a workaround used when state law is stricter.
It requires that property unlawfully seized in violation of the act be returned to its owner 'with all deliberate speed'.

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies that currently keep seized property and its proceeds to fund salaries, vehicles, and equipment, and that can route around state limits through federal sharing programs. Taxpayers in general are unaffected; the cost is borne by agencies' forfeiture revenue.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves criminal forfeiture intact — property can still be taken after a criminal conviction — so it abolishes the civil process rather than forfeiture entirely, and its exceptions for contraband and convicted owners would still require litigation over what counts.

Law enforcement agencies would lose forfeiture proceeds they currently use to fund salaries, vehicles, and equipment, and would lose the federal 'equitable sharing' workaround they can use when state law is stricter.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — ending a practice where property can be taken without a criminal conviction — is substantial and would fall on ordinary people, including innocent owners whose cash or cars are seized. The cost is real but narrower: law enforcement would lose a funding stream and would have to pursue forfeiture through criminal convictions, which the bill expressly allows. The bill's shortcoming is political, not design: it attracted no cosponsors and no committee action.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and Congress adjourned weeks later, so it expired with no vote.

narrative.text: Introduced December 10, 2014, with zero cosponsors and referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies keep the civil forfeiture powers and equitable-sharing revenue the bill would have ended; property owners remain subject to the existing system.

for.name: Rep. Steve Stockman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill abolishing federal civil asset forfeiture on December 10, 2014.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (113th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so no record exists of partisan support or opposition beyond its single Republican sponsor.

industries.industry: Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill would end a revenue stream: agencies can currently keep or sell seized property and share proceeds through federal 'equitable sharing' programs, funding salaries, vehicles, and equipment. Under the bill, forfeiture would require a criminal conviction or fall under narrow contraband exceptions.

industries.industry: Businesses whose cash or assets are seized (e.g., cash-intensive small businesses and travelers)
industries.note: This is the group the bill protects: owners would no longer have to sue to prove their own innocence to get property back. It is an interest group only in the sense of people targeted by current practice.
